sources.title: Indications for metabolic and bariatric surgery
Consensus statement: best practice guidelines based on experience of more than 12,000 cases
Guidelines for perioperative care in bariatric surgery: ERAS Society recommendations

indications: Obesity meeting the indications for metabolic and bariatric surgery after multidisciplinary assessment; the 2022 ASMBS and IFSO statement recommends surgery for BMI of 35 or more regardless of comorbidity, and consideration from BMI 30 with metabolic disease.
The same statement advises lower BMI thresholds in Asian populations; Indian surgeons should apply the thresholds their national and unit guidance has adopted.
Patients in whom a sleeve is the chosen operation after discussion of alternatives such as gastric bypass.
contraindications: Severe gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and Barrett's oesophagus, which a sleeve can worsen; a gastric bypass is often preferred.
Uncontrolled psychiatric illness, active substance misuse, or inability to engage with lifelong follow-up and supplementation.
Unfit for general anaesthesia and pneumoperitoneum.
Pregnancy, or pregnancy planned within the period of rapid weight loss.
preparation: Multidisciplinary assessment: surgeon, dietitian, psychologist and physician, with optimisation of diabetes, sleep apnoea and other comorbidities.
Screen for obstructive sleep apnoea (for example with STOP-Bang) and arrange treatment before surgery.
Upper endoscopy before surgery in many units, to assess reflux, hiatal hernia and Barrett's oesophagus.
A pre-operative low-energy diet to shrink the liver, according to unit practice.

Consent must include staple line leak, bleeding, stricture or twist of the sleeve, new or worse reflux, vitamin and mineral deficiencies, venous thromboembolism, inadequate weight loss or weight regain, injury to spleen, liver or bowel, conversion to open, and the irreversibility of the gastrectomy.
positioning: Supine on a bariatric-rated table, legs apart (French position) or surgeon on the right, according to unit practice.
Steep reverse Trendelenburg; secure the patient with footplates and straps before tilting.
Pad pressure areas carefully and use intermittent pneumatic compression devices.
equipment: Bariatric table, long laparoscopic instruments and extra-long ports.
Liver retractor, energy device, and a linear stapler with loads of staple heights suited to antral and fundal wall thickness.
Calibration bougie of the size the unit has standardised.
Methylene blue or endoscope for leak testing if used, and a retrieval bag.
anatomy: The greater curvature is supplied by the gastroepiploic arcade and, at the top, the short gastric vessels from the spleen.
The lesser curvature, which forms the sleeve, keeps its supply from the left and right gastric arteries.
The incisura angularis is the narrowest point of the lesser curvature and the common site of stenosis.
The angle of His lies between the fundus and the oesophagus; the gastro-oesophageal junction is the commonest leak site.
The posterior fundus is attached to the left crus and retroperitoneum; it must be fully freed so no fundus is left behind.
A hiatal hernia is common in this population and is looked for at operation.
criticalSafety: Communicate every bougie and tube movement with the anaesthetist; remove all other intragastric tubes before stapling.
Keep the incisura wide and the staple line straight and symmetrical.
Stay away from the gastro-oesophageal junction with the last firing.
Check the staple line for bleeding at normal blood pressure.
Look for and repair a hiatal hernia.
commonErrors: Narrowing at the incisura, causing functional obstruction.
Leaving posterior fundus, causing a fundal pouch and poor weight loss.
Spiralling or twisting the staple line.
Stapling too close to the junction.
Failing to recognise and repair a hiatal hernia.
complications: Staple line leak, most often near the gastro-oesophageal junction, presenting with tachycardia, fever or pain.
Stenosis or twist, causing dysphagia and vomiting.
Portomesenteric vein thrombosis and venous thromboembolism.
Nutritional deficiencies including iron, vitamin B12, folate, vitamin D and calcium.
Inadequate weight loss and weight regain.
postop: Enhanced recovery: early mobilisation, multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia, antiemetics, and early oral fluids according to unit protocol.
Treat persistent tachycardia, fever or new pain as a leak until proven otherwise; a heart rate threshold should be agreed by the unit.
Thromboprophylaxis per unit protocol, with consideration of extended prophylaxis after discharge in higher-risk patients.
Staged diet progression with dietitian support, acid suppression as advised, and lifelong vitamin and mineral supplementation and monitoring.
Continue CPAP for sleep apnoea, and arrange long-term follow-up in a bariatric service.

steps.emphasis: Confirm MDT approval, reflux assessment and the irreversibility of the operation.
State the bougie size, the stapler loads planned and who will manage the tubes.
Weight-adjusted antibiotic and thromboprophylaxis dosing per local protocol; mechanical prophylaxis from induction.
Bariatric table, footplates and straps before steep reverse Trendelenburg; check every pressure point.
Many bariatric surgeons use optical entry in the left upper quadrant; long ports and instruments are needed.
Divide the gastroepiploic branches close to the stomach from the starting point up to the angle of His, freeing the posterior fundus completely.
Inspect the hiatus; if a hiatal hernia is present, reduce it and expose both crura.
Only if a hiatal hernia is found.
Stop or convert for uncontrolled bleeding, a stapler misfire across the junction, or loss of orientation.
Test the sleeve with methylene blue via the orogastric tube or air under saline or endoscopy, according to unit practice.
Raise the blood pressure towards normal and inspect the whole staple line, the gastroepiploic bed and the spleen.
Close the extraction site and any 12 mm port fascia; this is difficult in a thick abdominal wall and a suture passer helps.
Record the start point, bougie size, staple loads, reinforcement, leak test result and any hiatal repair.

step.slv.start-point.title: Marking the antral starting point
step.slv.start-point.why: Where the resection starts decides how much antrum is kept. Starting too close to the pylorus narrows the outlet and raises pressure in the sleeve; starting too far away leaves a large antrum and less restriction.
how: Identify the pylorus by its vein and the thickened muscle, and measure along the greater curvature.
Start the greater curve dissection and the first firing at the distance the unit has standardised; the expert consensus describes a range of about 2 to 6 cm from the pylorus.
Mark the point with diathermy or a stitch so the whole team sees it before the first firing.
pitfalls: Starting the stapling at the pylorus itself.
Measuring along a stretched greater curve and starting too close.

step.slv.stapling.title: Stapling the sleeve along the bougie
step.slv.stapling.why: The staple line decides the shape of the sleeve and where it fails. Narrowing at the incisura causes functional obstruction and raises pressure; a staple line too close to the junction is the commonest site of leak; a spiralled line twists the sleeve.
how: With the bougie lying against the lesser curvature and confirmed in the antrum, fire the first loads across the antrum with a staple height suited to the thick antral wall, angled to keep the incisura wide.
Fire successive loads parallel to the bougie, keeping the anterior and posterior walls symmetrical: pull the stomach laterally evenly so neither wall is taken more than the other.
Approach the angle of His staying lateral to the gastro-oesophageal junction (commonly about 1 cm), so the junction is not narrowed or devascularised, and make sure no posterior fundus remains.
Before each firing, check the jaws are clear of the bougie, the nasogastric tube, any probe and the left crus, and that the stapler is closed fully before firing.
Inspect the staple line for bleeding and for any gaps where two lines cross; reinforce or oversew according to unit practice.
structuresAtRisk: Bougie and any other intragastric tube
Left gastric artery branches on the lesser curvature
pitfalls: Spiralling the staple line so the sleeve twists.
Stapling too close to the gastro-oesophageal junction.
Firing across a bougie or tube nobody had confirmed removed or positioned.
